entities.name: Marcus Genucius Augurinus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Marcus Genucius Augurinus, a patrician of the ancient Roman Genucia gens, served as consul in 451 BCE and was a pivotal member of the First Decemvirate, a commission established to codify Roman law. His tenure occurred during a critical period of constitutional upheaval in the early Roman Republic, marked by intense social friction between the patrician aristocracy and the plebeian majority. The Decemvirate's work laid the foundation for the Law of the Twelve Tables, a monumental legal code that profoundly shaped Roman jurisprudence and influenced Western legal traditions for millennia. His role, alongside his colleagues, represented a significant, albeit controversial, attempt to stabilize the nascent Republic by formalizing its legal framework.

In 451 BCE, following years of plebeian agitation for written laws to curb arbitrary patrician power, Marcus Genucius Augurinus was elected consul. Shortly thereafter, he and his consular colleague, Appius Claudius Crassus Inregillensis Sabinus, were appointed as the initial members of the First Decemvirate (Decemviri Legibus Scribundis), a ten-man commission granted supreme authority to draft a comprehensive legal code. This body, composed entirely of patricians, suspended all other magistracies, including the tribunes of the plebs, and governed Rome for a year. During their term, Genucius Augurinus participated in the creation of the first ten tables of what would become the Law of the Twelve Tables, which were publicly displayed in the Roman Forum for citizen review and approval. While the historical accounts of his specific individual contributions are sparse, his collective involvement was central to this foundational legal project.
